modern: How can our principles become dead, unless the thoughts which correspond to them are extinguished? But it is in your power to keep fanning these thoughts into a flame. I can have the opinion I ought to have about anything. If I can, why am I disturbed? The things which are outside my mind have no relation at all to my mind.—Let this be the state of your feelings, and you stand upright. To recover your life is in your power. Look at things again as you used to look at them; for in this lies the recovery of your life.
original: How can our principles become dead, unless the impressions [thoughts] which correspond to them are extinguished? But it is in thy power continuously to fan these thoughts into a flame. I can have that opinion about anything which I ought to have. If I can, why am I disturbed? The things which are external to my mind have no relation at all to my mind.—Let this be the state of thy affects, and thou standest erect. To recover thy life is in thy power. Look at things again as thou didst use to look at them; for in this consists the recovery of thy life.

explained.summary:
Your principles only die if you stop thinking about them, and keeping them alive is up to you, like fanning a fire. Marcus reminds himself that he can always form the right view of things, and that events outside his mind have no direct grip on it, so being disturbed is something he lets happen.

The hopeful part is the end: you can get your life back at any time simply by looking at things again the way you did when you saw them clearly.
explained.today: After a rough few weeks of skipped habits and short temper, you don’t need a grand reset. Rereading the notes, book or advice that once steadied you, and looking at your situation through it again, is often enough to find your footing.
